pages.text: A $(thing)Crucible$() is a ceramic pot for melting metal and mixing $(l:metalworking/crucible#advanced_alloying)Alloys$() in exact proportions: it is better for that than a $(l:getting_started/primitive_alloys)Small Vessel$(). It is made of $(l:metalworking/fire_clay)Fire Clay$(), knapped to shape and then fired.

Fire it at 1300 °C: in a $(l:metalworking/charcoal_forge)Charcoal Forge$() with bellows, not in a pit kiln. At work it needs heat from below, usually a forge, or from above, from a $(l:metalworking/blast_furnace)Blast Furnace$().
A crucible on a charcoal forge.
Using the crucible opens its interface. The top shows the metal inside: the first named is what you would draw off now, the others make up the mix.
pages.title: Alloying

pages.text: Nine slots take items to melt, and the liquid goes into the pot. Molds and vessels of molten metal drain into it slowly, which gives exact mixes: hold $(item)$(k:key.sneak)$() over one to hurry it. A mold or vessel in the output slot is filled from the pot.

Native metals, malachite and cassiterite melt into metal. Sulfide ores roast instead, and give off fumes where the pot stands: tetrahedrite gives arsenical copper, bismuthinite gives bismuth, galena gives work lead, sphalerite gives a calcine and no zinc, which needs a retort. Iron ore melts only into an oxide that cannot be cast. See $(l:tfcpp/sulfides)Sulfide Ores and the Retort$(), $(l:tfcpp/lead_silver)Lead and Silver$() and $(l:tfcpp/iron_phosphorus)Iron and Phosphorus$().
pages.title: What melts

pages.text: The temperature gauge follows the heat source below or above. Metal can be drawn off while it is still molten. A broken crucible keeps its contents, so a full one can be carried. Wrought iron melts at 1535 °C and steel at 1520 °C.
